title: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?
description: The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khr
body:
The Venice Film Festival found itself under fire in the weeks leading up to opening night over the inclusion of “DAU,” by Russian filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky, in the main competition of its 83rd edition.

	In a joint statement released on Aug. 17, the Ukraine Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Culture and the Ukrainian Embassy in Italy criticized the prestigious fest for selecting what they claimed to be “a project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence,” maintaining that the decision helped to “restore respectability” to Putin’s pariah state.
	

	The pushback was swift. In an Instagram post responding to the criticism, Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera insisted that “‘DAU’ is not a Russian film; it is not pro-Putin propaganda.” Meanwhile, Khrzhanovsky took to Facebook to refute allegations that the latest installment in his long-running project was backed by Russian financing or is “an instrument of Russian state cultural policy.” 

	Speaking to Variety on the eve of the festival, the director doubled down, saying: “Since the war started, there was no question of what side I am on, because I am on the side of Ukraine.”

	Coming on the heels of a recent controversy surrounding the Venice Art Biennale’s decision to mount shows by Russian and Israeli artists, the “DAU” dust-up speaks to a larger question hanging over film festivals, cultural institutions and other events that, in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, largely heeded calls for a boycott of Russian cultural exports.
	

	As the war drags deeper into its fifth year, a rapprochement of sorts is underway. While relations with Moscow remain frosty for much of the world, Russian filmmakers are gradually coming in from the cold.

	In the past year alone, Russian-born directors have scooped prizes in Venice (Nastia Korkia’s “Short Summer”) and Cannes (Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur”), while Khrzhanovsky is joined on the Lido by fellow exile Victor Kossakovsky, whose latest documentary, “Holly Wood Dust,” premieres out of competition. 

	Though the Oscar-nominated Kossakovsky (“Gunda”) and Khrzhanovsky both left Russia in the 2000s, a broader exodus began not long after Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine in February 2022. Whether fleeing in protest of the Kremlin’s war machine or out of fear of the brutal crackdown on dissent that quickly followed, many of Russian cinema’s most prominent voices left the country, forging exile communities from Tbilisi to Paris, from Berlin to L.A.

	“There are two Russias right now,” says two-time Oscar nominee Alexander Rodnyansky (“Leviathan”), in Venice with Kornél Mundruczó’s “Place to Be,” starring Ellen Burstyn and Taika Waititi. “Russia as the country with this regime controlling everything and censoring all the attempts to speak freely about what’s going on. And there is a Russia outside of the geographical borders.”

	That diaspora is experiencing exile in a variety of ways. The Kyiv-born Rodnyansky, who was sentenced in absentia to 8.5 years in prison by a Moscow court over his opposition to the war, remains determined to support dissenting voices and “make movies with Russian filmmakers, especially young ones, who I feel myself committed to help.” Now based in France, Zvyagintsev likewise remains a trenchant critic of a country he says he has “no intention” of returning to. Though filmed in Latvia, his Cannes Grand Prix-winning “Minotaur” is as scathing a portrait of Russian society under Putin as the director’s previous works.

	For other filmmakers, the westward flight has offered an opportunity for reinvention. Kantemir Balagov’s “Butterfly Jam,” which opened the Directors’ Fortnight section this year in Cannes, stars Barry Keoghan and Riley Keough and is set in an immigrant community in Newark. Director Kirill Sokolov likewise set off for Hollywood; his latest, the blood-soaked revenge farce “They Will Kill You,” stars Zazie Beetz and Patricia Arquette.
	

	Sokolov’s dark comedy “No Looking Back” was among the first films to bear the brunt of the anti-Russia backlash in 2022, when it was pulled from the Glasgow Film Festival over financing that came in part from the Putin regime. The “DAU” controversy in Venice was similarly driven by ties to Russian financiers who would later be sanctioned following the Ukraine invasion.

	But Khrzhanovsky stresses to Variety that their involvement in his decades-spanning project ended years ago; his Venice-bound film is a German production, co-produced with France and Sweden, and has received no Russian funding for seven years, according to the director. 

	As these and other Russian filmmakers set up new lives in exile, the financial ties that once bound them to Putin’s state have been cut. That, as much as their vocal opposition to the Ukraine war, arguably weakens the case for protest and will ease further reentry into the international film community. 

	“They’re shot in Europe. They’re financed in Europe,” says Laurent Danielou, of Paris-based Loco Films, who’s currently financing two features from émigré Russian directors. “They’re not Russian anymore.”

schema.headline: Are Russian Filmmakers Finally Coming in From the Cold?

title: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’
description: Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival, where her feature-lengt
body:
Roma filmmaker Alina Șerban broke barriers long before she set foot on the red carpet this week at the Venice Film Festival, where her feature-length directorial debut, “I Matter,” world premieres in the Venice Spotlight section.

	Rising from an impoverished background to become a celebrated stage star in Romania, the actress and directing debutante has defied all odds to reach the starry heights of the Lido. Billed as the first feature from a female Roma director to screen at an A-list festival, “I Matter” marks the latest chapter in her life-long quest to reframe the narrative around her marginalized community. 
	

	Șerban, however, is taking it all in stride.


	“I’m nervous about the pressure of being ‘the first’ — all the firsts,” she tells Variety. “But I also have this immense relief, and the feeling of being grateful that I managed to pull through something almost impossible.”

	Inspired by Șerban’s own life, “I Matter” tells the story of a young Roma woman studying to be an actor. She’s faced with the threat of being kicked out of her orphanage and must suddenly embrace her identity and confront the reality of making it through life on her own. Based on the 2021 short of the same name, whose festival run included New Directors/New Films, it’s produced by microFILM, 2Pilots Filmproduction, Frakas Prods. and Lemming Film, with international sales handled by Pluto Film.

	For Șerban, the premiere is a capstone in what has already been a remarkable career. Raised in poverty in Bucharest, she was placed in a state-run orphanage at an early age before becoming the first member of her family to graduate from high school. After attending Bucharest’s Academy of Theatrical Arts and Cinematography, she was accepted into NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts, then later earned a master’s degree from the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London.
	

	When she returned to Romania, she mounted an acclaimed one-woman show about her life, focusing not only on the rampant discrimination she faced, but on her triumphs and joys. By her 30th birthday, Șerban had written and staged pioneering plays that championed a radical, feminist, Roma perspective — trying, she says, “to show the humanity of these people. Not to portray them as victims nor villains. Not to self-exoticize. But also to celebrate ourselves.”

	“I Matter” stars newcomer Denisa Farcaș, bringing both vulnerability and determination to a lead role that she invests with her own life experience, according to the director. Șerban describes working with Farcaș and her co-stars as a “collaborative process,” one in which the group delved deep into “what it means to be accepted” as Roma women while giving the young actors space to “express themselves — to feel that they also own the story.”

	This isn’t Șerban’s first visit to the Venice Film Festival; she attended in 2023 with the cast and crew of Goran Stolevski’s “Housekeeping for Beginners,” in which she had a supporting role. But this year’s experience will be something else entirely for the director. Nearly two dozen of the cast members of “I Matter” will be in attendance — including the 16 child performers who populated the film’s orphanage — while Roma band Mahala Rai Banda will serenade the red-carpet arrivals.

	“This is such a historical moment for me, and also for the Roma community,” Șerban says. “It’s a moment of celebration. And I want to look back and say I did everything in my power for the people in the team to [share this] moment. And also to put into the world a message of dignity, of celebration, of pain that needs to be seen.”

schema.headline: Groundbreaking Roma Director Alina Șerban on ‘Pain,’ ‘Joy,’ of Historic, Venice-Bound ‘I Matter’: ‘I Managed to Do Something Impossible’

title: Bad Bunny Wins Emmy for Super Bowl Halftime Show
description:
Bad Bunny has won his first Emmy for the Super Bowl Halftime Show. He won in the outstanding variety special (live) category.

	“The Apple Music Sup
body:
Bad Bunny has won his first Emmy for the Super Bowl Halftime Show. He won in the outstanding variety special (live) category.

	“The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny” took home a total of seven nominations, winning music direction, choreography, sound mixing, lighting design, technical direction/camerawork and directing.

	Jay-Z, also an executive producer on the show, won his third Emmy.

	Bad Bunny and the event’s producers and directors pulled off what may have been the most intricate halftime extravaganza in Super Bowl history. Superstar guests included Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin, a real-life wedding and authentic business owners (including Los Angeles’ own Villa’s Tacos) among the set.
	

	Speaking about the performance, creative director Harriet Cuddeford previously told Variety, “The performance is celebrating normal people, and what it is to be human and love and have joy, and really appreciate one another. This was to show how much he values his community, to celebrate normal people on the world’s biggest stage, especially people who are of importance in Latino culture. He’s a very authentic person, Benito, and it’s about just being authentic and very real and very human.”

schema.headline: Bad Bunny Wins Emmy for Super Bowl Halftime Show

title: Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Watermelon Pictures has acquired “Everything Is Not OK,” a documentary from director Dev Benegal chronicling the life of artist Judith Blum Reddy.
body:
Watermelon Pictures has acquired “Everything Is Not OK,” a documentary from director Dev Benegal chronicling the life of artist Judith Blum Reddy. 

	The film will stream exclusively on Watermelon+, the distributor’s streaming platform.

	The producing team pairs Benegal with Min(d) Studio’s Maya S. Patel and Neeraj Jain, while Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36”) has signed on as executive producer.


	“Everything Is Not OK” follows Reddy, whose work as an artist has been shaped by the Holocaust and by displacements that carried her from New York to Paris and ultimately India. The documentary threads Reddy’s story together with those of fellow artists Nil Yalter, Zarina and Camille Billops, each of whom channeled displacement into their art. Palestinian, Kashmiri and Indian poets are interwoven throughout, framing the film as a meditation on remembering what has been erased from home and pushing back once staying quiet stops being an option.
	

	“For Judy, making art is an act of confrontation. An act of liberation. A refusal to let erasure win,” Benegal said. “‘Everything Is Not OK’ is not only a portrait of an artist — it is a meditation on what it means to create, remember and resist through art when silence is no longer an option.”

	Jacir signed on as executive producer after connecting with the film’s exploration of memory and resistance. “In a moment when the world tilts towards intolerance, Judy’s story is a reminder that memory refuses to disappear and art can still be an act of resistance,” Jacir said.

	Jacir and actor Adam Bakri both lend their voices to the film’s readings of revolutionary poetry.
	

	Benegal is also known for directing “English, August” and “Road, Movie.” A restored version of “English, August,” undertaken by the Film Heritage Foundation, is playing at the Venice Film Festival. The 1994 film is based on Upamanyu Chatterjee’s novel “English, August: An Indian Story” and stars Rahul Bose.

	The creative team behind “Everything Is Not OK” includes Jain doubling as producer and additional cinematography; Patel as producer; Dhruv Goel composing the music; Jean-Luc Panda as cinematographer; Mona Gesbel as editor; Anurag Jadhao on sound design; and Rob Sciarratta as colorist.

	Watermelon Pictures launched in 2024. Its distribution and production credits include “From Ground Zero” and “All That’s Left of You” alongside “Palestine 36,” all three shortlisted in the Academy Award’s international feature category, plus the Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” Hamza Ali and co-founder Badie Ali brought the Watermelon+ platform online in May 2025, positioning it as the largest single collection of Palestinian film ever assembled in one place.

title: ‘Elsinore’ Revisits Daniel Day-Lewis’ Infamous Walk-Off During ’80s ‘Hamlet’ Production
description: Audiences got the first glimpse at a triumphant and career-defining performance from Andrew Scott in “Elsinore” this weekend, but the Telluride play
body:
Audiences got the first glimpse at a triumphant and career-defining performance from Andrew Scott in “Elsinore” this weekend, but the Telluride player also delivers another important gift: legendary show business gossip.

	Central to the plot is an infamous real-life moment in the history of the U.K. theater — when Daniel Day-Lewis stopped cold during a performance of “Hamlet,” before stalking off stage and never coming back. Ever.
	

	“Elsinore” opens in 1989, during a production of “Hamlet” at London’s National Theater. During a fraught encounter between Hamlet and the ghost of his father, an actor freezes before exiting entirely. The incident shocks audience members and sends cast and crew into a meltdown.


	“That’s not supposed to happen,” deadpans a sassy house manager, watching the disaster unfold in real time on CCTV. Director Simon Stone’s camera follows the actor as he storms to his dressing room, where a slammed door reveals Day-Lewis’ name on a placard. The Telluride crowd erupted in laughter and surprise at the reveal. It reminded (or informed) them that it happened in the first place.

	“Elsinore” is the heart-wrenching true story of Scottish actor Ian Charelson. The star of “Chariots of Fire” had the chance of a lifetime to replace Day-Lewis as Hamlet in that same production, all while succumbing to complications from end-stage AIDS. He died 7 weeks after bowing out to rave reviews. Filmmakers and producers on “Elsinore” approached the matter sensitively, numerous sources told Variety, and screened a rough cut of the film for Day-Lewis’ reps before the Telluride premiere to get their blessing.
	

	So what happened on that fateful November day in 1989? Actors, academics and press are still trying to solve the puzzle 37 years later. The British media devoured the story, as even then Day-Lewis was synonymous with intense devotion to his craft. Urban legend goes that Day-Lewis saw the ghost of his own late father, the poet Cecil Day-Lewis, that night on stage. In 2012, the “Lincoln” star debunked this myth (though he gave quotes at the time that supported the supernatural anecdote). 

	That year was incredibly fraught for Day-Lewis. He’d wrapped production on “My Left Foot” and was barreling toward his first ever Academy Award, one he’d win four months later at the Dorothy Chandler Pavillion in 1990. The same year as the “Hamlet” debacle, he’d also met French actress Isabelle Adjani, with who he reportedly had a tumultuous relationship before a breakup in 1996.

	“I work in a certain way, and I never really felt the need to explain it or apologize for it, but in England, they thought I was unhinged,” Day-Lewis told Time magazine in 2012. “The press goes after you, and they don’t tend to let go.”

	On the ground in Telluride, we caught up with “Elsinore” producer Gabrielle Tana, who says the moment ultimately reinforces Charelson’s destiny.

	 “It was the dream come true. It was carpe diem, and he got an opportunity to do the thing that he always wanted to do,. Ian felt he was washed up, and all of a sudden this gift was there for him,” said Tana.

	Focus Features will release “Elsinore” in theaters on Nov. 20.

schema.headline: ‘Elsinore’ Revisits Daniel Day-Lewis’ Infamous Walk-Off During ’80s ‘Hamlet’ Production

title: San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Paris-based Moveria has boarded international sales on Taiwanese filmmaker Lu Po-Shun’s debut feature “Will You Still Be My Friend,” which is set fo
body:
Paris-based Moveria has boarded international sales on Taiwanese filmmaker Lu Po-Shun’s debut feature “Will You Still Be My Friend,” which is set for a berth in San Sebastián’s New Directors sidebar before travelling on to the Busan International Film Festival.

	A Taiwan-Singapore co-production, the film follows two young boys, played by Jaden Wang and Aloysius Looi, whose bond comes under strain as tensions build between their families and the surrounding rural community. Rounding out the cast are Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang and Xing Chang.
	

	A trailer has been unveiled.


	Eric Chou Tseng-Chen and Yu-Hao Su produced the film through Taiwan-based InLight Film Studio and Verdant Peak Films.

	At San Sebastián, the film is also in contention for the Sebastiane Award, an honor for films exploring LGBTQIA+ themes and experiences.

	In the story, an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village forces a boy to shield his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend from the adult conflicts threatening to divide them, even as he privately begins to question his own feelings for his friend.

	“What I really connected with is the relationship between the two boys,” said Yasmin Porangaba, Moveria’s head of sales and acquisition. “When they’re alone, everything feels simple, light and natural. It’s like they have this little world of their own, almost like a secret, because the people around them don’t really get them. Around their families and friends, they have to fit into certain roles, while their time together feels like a space where none of that matters.
	

	“I also love that the film never defines what they are to each other. They’re too young to really make sense of it themselves, and I like that the film leaves that open. They know how to be there for each other, forgive each other and just move forward in a way that feels surprisingly mature. The two boys are amazing together, the film is beautiful, and that’s really what made us want to represent it.”

	The film has already built an international industry profile through selections including Ties That Bind, the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion, EFM Far East in Progress and HAF Goes to Cannes at the Cannes Film Market.

	Lu’s short film “Wild Tides” earlier earned him the best director prize at the Taipei Film Awards. He also directed the segment “Way Home” in the 2018 anthology film “Ten Years Taiwan,” part of Busan’s A Window on Asian Cinema lineup. “Will You Still Be My Friend” is his first feature as director.

	Producer Eric Chou Tseng-Chen brings experience in sales, acquisitions, project management and festival promotion on the international circuit, and co-produced “Get the Hell Out,” which had its bow in the Midnight Madness lineup at Toronto in 2020.

	Yu-Hao Su has produced credits such as Shatara Michelle Ford’s “Test Pattern,” a Film Independent Spirit Award and Gotham Award nominee, as well as “Fragrance of the First Flower.” Su also executive produced Ford’s “Dreams in Nightmares,” which screened in Berlinale’s Panorama section.

	InLight Film Studio, a Taiwan-based outfit, spans film and visual art projects, while Verdant Peak Films is dedicated to bringing Taiwanese stories to global audiences and developing international co-productions. Verdant Peak’s recent credits include “Dreams in Nightmares.”

	Moveria, headquartered in Paris, operates as an independent production and sales outfit for international markets.

	Watch the trailer here:

schema.headline: San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’
description: For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black
body:
For Lucy Liu, who has voiced memorable characters in everything from “Kung Fu Panda” to “Strange World,” being part of the independently made, black-and-white animated film “Moonfish” was all about lending her name and support to first-time filmmaker Daniel Zvereff.

	“These are the people that are not just the creatives, but the ones who are going to be the future,” Liu tells Variety. “I’m just fascinated by how people work and how things start when there’s not all this red tape.”
	

	Premiering at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 6 after receiving a grant from Biennale College Cinema, “Moonfish” follows a pair of astronauts, voiced by Liu and “The Gilded Age” star Morgan Spector, as they embark on an isolating mission to the moon with a corporate quota to meet if they want to return home.


	“I really wanted to have the film take place in an environment that was an allegory to our current human condition we’re all experiencing right now, where society is very plugged in, but simultaneously we’re all growing a bit disconnected,” Zvereff says.

	Zvereff designed the 2D-animated film so that he could finish it completely on his own, if need be. Thankfully, as Zvereff worked over the course of nine months, he managed to bring on two animators, Hoss Wheeler and Devin Grover.

	“When I watch 2D-animated films, I feel like I’m being exposed to the subconscious of that artist,” Zvereff says of his approach.

	Liu adds, “It’s amazing what digital has done for the speed of animation but you can really feel the appreciation and the craftsmanship [here]. There is a tenderness and an imperfection that I appreciate.”
	

	Unlike Liu, Spector had never done an animated film before “Moonfish.” The trickiest part was getting into his character’s mental headspace as he goes “a little mad,” as Spector puts it.

	“This particular class of people has come to live on the moon, and they’ve evolved, essentially, as moon people. But they’ve also evolved as an underclass; they are the group of people without rights, assets or any real hope for the future,” Spector says of Zvereff’s worldbuilding.

	Liu, of course, also voices the talking fish that accompanies the pair (which Zvereff likens to how miners brought along canaries to know when they had to leave) amidst the mundanity of the corporate tasks at hand.

	“The future that Daniel’s imagining is one in which the relationship between human beings and their tools has been totally inverted. The corporation has merged with the computer in a sort of perfect authoritarian machine that uses human beings as fodder, basically,” Spector says. “It’s a vision of the world that feels continuous with the one we live in.”

	While the film explores isolation and loneliness in space, with the dialogue sparse and to-the-point, Zvereff realized during the writing process that it needed to ultimately be positive about the future of humanity.

	“That’s something that happens as an artist. When you’re making something, you’re taking in all these feelings you’re happening and running them through this prism,” he says. “And out comes this beautiful, unexpected light.”

schema.headline: Moonfish’ Director and Stars Lucy Liu and Morgan Spector Break Down Their Black-and-White Animated Film About Isolated Astronauts And Why It’s an Allegory for ‘The Current Human Condition’

title: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore Is Astonishing in Jesse Eisenberg’s Funny and Dizzying Community-Theater Comedy
description: It’s rare these days to find comedy and humanity on the same plate — and even more rare to see comedy nuzzling up to mystery. (I don’t mean mystery
body:
It’s rare these days to find comedy and humanity on the same plate — and even more rare to see comedy nuzzling up to mystery. (I don’t mean mystery as in crime-solving; I mean the mystery of existence.) But Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” a small-town-theater comedy driven by big ideas, is a funny and dizzying mind-bender. It’s like “Waiting for Guffman” made by the Coen brothers at their most rivetingly unhinged. “The Debut” won’t be for everyone, but if you get onto its wavelength (which I did immediately), it sucks you into its “Twilight Zone of Sub-Broadway” vortex, even as the tone remains light and ticklish and surprising.
	

	Eisenberg, as he proved two years ago in the brilliant “A Real Pain,” is a grounded filmmaker (he loves reality). But here he’s working on a high wire of matter-of-fact satire that edges, just barely, into the surreal. Yet it’s still reality-based. At heart, the film is a twisted love letter to the glory of community theater. What holds it together is the suppleness of Eisenberg’s voice as a writer-director (the wit that singes, the story that never stops poking around corners), and the utterly astonishing performance of Julianne Moore, who plays a crumpled wallflower in dire need of blooming. Oh, does she bloom.


	Moore’s Mona Friedman is a New Jersey homemaker who has become a Stepford zombie, because no one seems to need her anymore. Her twins, Matty (Joan Diamand) and Maya (Becca Suskauer), are nearly adults, and though they’re still living at home they’ve already checked out. Her husband, Howard (Patrick Fabian), is a handsome stiff-necked jerk who treats Mona like an accessory. And she’s such a fearful, passive people pleaser that none of this is in any danger of changing. Moore, with red eyes and translucent skin, gives off the aura of a damaged doll.
	

	In the opening scene, set in the Brook Theater, she tries out for a small role in the annual local production of “Nosy Neighbors,” and her audition is so weak that we don’t see how she could possibly get the part. She doesn’t. It goes instead to Serena Cherry (Bernadette Peters), a Broadway wannabe who lands any role she wants. (There’s a poster of her in the lobby as the lead in a production of “Evita.”) But then, late one night, Mona gets a call from the musical’s director, Jerry (Paul Giamatti). Serena has bowed out; he’s got no one else to do the part. So Mona is in. (It helps that she ripped off all the phone-number tags on a local flyer for the audition.)

	Mona comes into rehearsal the next morning (the cast has been at it for several weeks), and what we instantly see is that “Nosy Neighbors,” an upbeat musical about the residents of a downscale apartment building, is a corny but oddly sturdy piece of third-rate hokum – it’s like “Rent” redone by Corky St. Clair. (The songs, which Eisenberg composed, sound like Jonathan Larson-by-numbers.) Mona is playing Miss Danielle, the building super, a tough nut who wears a tool belt and has the signature line, “Rent’s due!” Not exactly an acting challenge.

	The other cast members are warm and welcoming, but Mona, who has no theatrical experience (beyond singing in her church choir until she was 13), is awful beyond words. She delivers that line as if she was whispering it in a library. She’s a doormat in life and a washout of an actress, even for community theater.

	So Jerry, realizing that he’s got a potential disaster on his hands, decides that his only recourse is to give Mona a tough-love private acting lesson. In a remarkable scene, he makes her ask for the rent check he’s holding in his hand — and more than that, he keeps asking her why she wants it, breaking down her defenses. It’s like a Sanford Meisner exercise turned torture session, and Mona finally busts through with a monologue that spills out of her guts, about how she wants that rent money because if she doesn’t get it she’ll be in an alley eating plague-ridden rats. She burns through her own lack of purpose and identity and, at that moment, becomes an actress. What Jerry doesn’t realize is that he’s created a monster.
	

	“The Debut” is at once an affectionate homage to the wide-eyed passion of community theater; a deftly original thriller; a parable of self-esteem; a teasing mockery of the mechanisms of self-esteem; and a one-woman psychodrama in which Mona discovers who she is by leaving her old reality behind.

	There’s a hilarious scene in which Jerry, as part of Mona’s Method training, takes her out to a random apartment building, and she talks her way into someone’s home by impersonating the super and demanding to fix the toilet. The thing is, the Method training works. Mona lets herself go and becomes a confident actress. Yet if that’s all there was to it, “The Debut” would just be a tidy feel-good fable. Eisenberg is too talented and ambitious to make that kind of movie. He wants instead to make our heads spin by taking us down a rabbit hole.

	It’s when Mona, fed up with her husband, moves out of her home and into a fleabag hotel, where the faucets drip and the dingy electric lights are buzzy and there are strange sounds coming through the walls, that the film begins to turn into a slightly dreamy hellscape. But Moore keeps us on her side. Her Mona is avid to find a new way to be, even if that means putting on a janitor suit and, after shorting out the hotel’s electricity (and burning off her eyebrows), getting a new look that makes her resemble Camille Paglia crossed with Joan Jett as styled by David Lynch. The joke, and it’s a juicy one, is that she has now gone full Method, and insists that everything her character in the musical says must be entirely reality-based.

	It wouldn’t work if Mona’s fearless new acting ethos weren’t so goddamn funny. And it wouldn’t work if Paul Giamatti, who’s kind of playing the audience’s surrogate, didn’t invest Jerry, the disgruntled theater romantic, with a hope and rage and bone-deep melancholy that keeps the film from flying off into the ether. The actors playing the song-and-dance cast members of “Nosy Neighbors” (they include Eisenberg) perform with sublimely subtle cluelessness. But it’s the audacity of Julianne Moore — now clenched, now grinning, now timid, now acting — that brings “The Debut” to its gratifying conclusion, as Mona, through the theater, discovers an extraordinary new role: herself.

schema.headline: ‘The Debut’ Review: Julianne Moore Is Astonishing in Jesse Eisenberg’s Funny and Dizzying Community-Theater Comedy

title: Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’
description: Every great love story, in Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong‘s telling, is secretly a story about love that cannot happen — class, status or fate standin
body:
Every great love story, in Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong‘s telling, is secretly a story about love that cannot happen — class, status or fate standing in the way. His new film dares to ask the opposite question, and it took him the better part of two decades, one abandoned script about a 2009 workers’ strike and a single idea from his co-writer to find an answer worth filming.

	“When we think about a love story, usually the most typical love story we think about is love that cannot come true,” Lee says about Venice competition title “Possible Love,” his first feature since 2018’s “Burning.” “So to simply put it, you could say that all of these love stories are called impossible love, so to speak.”
	

	“Possible Love” follows Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), who works at a mask factory while dealing with the fallout of her husband Ho-seok’s (Sul Kyung-gu) layoff and the strike that followed it. A funeral draws the couple into contact with Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a filmmaker shooting a documentary about laid-off workers, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung); they are a couple whose money and detachment set them apart from Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s daily struggle. Once Mi-ok signs on to be filmed, a bond forms with Ye-ji, while something harder to name pulls her toward the unreadable Sang-woo, and the two households’ collision starts to crack open both marriages. Zo and Cho are working with Lee for the first time.


	The mass layoff at the center of the film happened at a major Korean company in 2009, followed by a 70-day strike and a violent crackdown by authorities. Lee began developing a fictional treatment soon after but could not finish it. “Every time I create a film, what I need is a conviction that this story is worth telling in the format of a film,” he says, adding that he could never settle whether turning real workers’ pain into fiction, rather than documentary, would mean anything to him, to audiences or to cinema itself. So he shelved it.
	

	The story only came back to life once his co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, suggested pairing it with the story of a filmmaker. “Because it is told adjacent to my own story as a filmmaker, I could be more honest in the storytelling,” Lee says, describing the addition as a new layer that gave him a way back in.

	That doubling lets him ask a question he says has followed him since his years as a novelist, long before he started directing. “When we deal with the lives of other people, are we worthy of telling their story, and are we not only using it for our own purposes? This is something that always I had in mind,” he says, adding that the question belongs to all filmmaking, not only documentaries, and that he wanted “Possible Love” to put it to the audience as much as to himself.

	He locates the film’s title in the same territory. “In our film, ‘Possible Love,’ as you can see in the title, it asks a question: what is love that is possible?” he says, noting that the love in question reaches beyond the romantic, to Ye-ji’s pull toward the people she films and to Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s marriage. On the distance between the two couples, he resists calling it simple class conflict: “Now we live at a time where class is really no longer just class,” he says, pointing to Sang-woo as someone who “deals with the amount of wealth and capital that is unfathomable by people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok.”

	Lee also traces the story to the 10th commandment, “thou shalt not covet,” and to Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10.” “The former nine [commandments] all are about human actions. However, this very last one is about the human heart,” he says, framing the film’s real question as how much resistance to coveting is even possible “in this capitalist society we live today,” and noting that Ye-ji’s desire to claim other people’s lives for her documentary is its own version of the same impulse.

	Jeon, reuniting with Lee nearly 20 years after “Secret Sunshine,” found her way into Mi-ok through what they share rather than their circumstances. “I thought that the anxiety she harbors in her heart was something that I could relate to, because I also have that as well,” she says, describing Mi-ok as someone living with “a ticking time bomb in her heart.” She had read Mi-ok’s pull toward Sang-woo as desire on the page, then revised that once shooting began. “I came to think that it’s more about curiosity,” she says.
	

	She also connected with Mi-ok’s refusal to collapse under hardship, echoing something she says has been said about her own work as an actor. “I don’t think that she is going to crumble and just be sad,” Jeon says, calling the character someone who won’t “let go of hope.” Stepping back onto Lee’s set after two decades felt easier than she expected. Where “Secret Sunshine” had been “very intense,” she says this time “I felt so comfortable and so much at ease when I stepped onto the set.” She adds that “Possible Love” arrives at a point in her career when she has grown frustrated watching commercial appeal crowd out character work in the Korean industry, and that the project is “so significant for me at this juncture.”

	Sul, reuniting with Lee 24 years after “Oasis,” which won Lee the Venice Film Festival‘s best director prize in 2002, agreed to the project before reading a script. “I think just the name Lee Chang-dong means complete trust for me,” he says, adding that “Peppermint Candy,” their first film together, remains the role he still calls his most representative work. Getting back on set stirred the same nerves he felt making that film decades earlier. “I just feel like all of this is the power that director Lee holds,” he says.

	Playing Ho-seok’s silence, he says, was the harder task. He describes the character as carrying rage, guilt and shame after being laid off, his pride “thrown on the ground,” with only “silence and just glances” as tools, all beneath an outwardly unbothered exterior. Asked whether he saw himself in the role, Sul calls Ho-seok “a universal Korean man,” caught between a tough exterior and a wound he never lets show. He’s less certain how much that particular tension has shifted since “Peppermint Candy”: “It has been three decades, so I do think there has been some changes,” he says, though he stops short of generalizing about Korean masculinity broadly.

	Lee, asked about Korean cinema’s rise since his 1997 debut “Green Fish,” when he says international interest in Korean film was “close to none,” credits the industry’s current global standing to younger filmmakers, adding that how optimistic to be about its future “is a question not for me to discuss, but something that I do believe the younger filmmakers of today should be asking themselves.”
	

	“Possible Love” heads next to the Toronto, Busan and London film festivals. It opens theatrically on Oct. 23 before streaming on Netflix starting Nov. 6.

schema.headline: Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’

title: Wim Wenders on Why He Made a Documentary About Architect Peter Zumthor, and How Brad Pitt Helped Get It Made
description: Wim Wenders’ 3D documentary “From Inside Out,” which has its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, examines the work of Pritzker Pri
body:
Wim Wenders’ 3D documentary “From Inside Out,” which has its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, examines the work of Pritzker Prize-winning architect Peter Zumthor, paying particular attention to the design and construction of the David Geffen Galleries of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.



	In the film, the result of a 14-year collaboration with the architect, Zumthor explains how he approaches the design of his buildings so that they are in harmony with their surroundings and serve the people who will use them.
	

	Wenders first came across Zumthor’s work when the architect took part in a competition for a gallery building in Berlin, opposite the Neues Museum. “It looked splendid but wasn’t built,” Wenders explains.


	Among those appearing in the film are filmmakers Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog, actress Ever Anderson, singer-songwriter Sophie Hunger, visual artist Tarek Atoui, and actress and dancer Aoi Yamada, who also appeared in Wenders’ “Perfect Days.” Brad Pitt serves as executive producer on the film. 

	Variety submitted a series of questions to the director about the film, and publishes his written responses below:

	When did you first meet Peter Zumthor?As a commission for the 13th Architecture Biennale, I made a short film on him: “Notes From a Day in the Life of an Architect.” We got along great and decided to do “something real” together, a long feature film.

	What motivated you to make a film about him?I have loved architecture since my childhood and always wanted to know more about the work of an architect. Zumthor seemed like an ideal partner, as his work is truly rethinking the very basis of what architecture is or can be.
	

	What was it about his architecture that made it a suitable subject for a film?The fact that Zumthor works in quite a radical way. He spends more time on each building than most of his colleagues, both in the design and the construction process. Like other artists, he feels that a building is not done or finished with the approved plans, but that it is shaped only in its construction process. As a filmmaker, I share that approach.

	Why did you choose to shoot it as a 3D film?No visual language would be more suitable for architecture than 3D.

	Can you speak about the role of the people in the film? Are they actors?They are not “actors.” They are real people who visit the buildings by Peter Zumthor or live in them. They see these places, and the audience sees and experiences them through their eyes.

	Was the construction of the David Geffen Galleries pivotal to the film?Absolutely. We had already started the film when the building of the new LACMA became real and was no longer just a project. Peter and I agreed that the film should definitely include this milestone in his career, and what was already a “long-term observation” now became even longer. I also met Brad Pitt at that moment, as he had been an ardent defender of Zumthor’s building, even in front of the City Council, and he agreed to help make the film.

	Can you explain how Zumthor contributed to the making of the film?We shot countless times with Zumthor over a period of 14 years, both in his office in Switzerland as well as all over the world. He always made himself available for our film, opened his archives and answered each and every one of my questions.

            Jay-Z fans may have come to see him perform ... but they ended up being performers themselves -- because he had them serenade Beyoncé!
      
    
            The rapper played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Friday as part of his limited tour engagement celebrating the 30th anniversary of his album "Reasonable Doubt" and the 25th anniversary of "The Blueprint."
      
    
      
      Jay-Z pauses his London show to have the massive crowd sing happy birthday to Beyoncé on her 45th birthday. 🎤 pic.twitter.com/b6tvg4hKwo
              @hiphopcnation
          
  
    
            In the middle of the show, Jay-Z stopped ... and told the crowd he wanted them to sing 'HBD' to his lady -- who turned 45 on Friday.
      

            Check out the vid ... fireworks start exploding, and the band strikes up a song -- before thousands of voices scream out the track with Jay leading them.
      
    
            Bey looks overjoyed ... clearly shocked about her man's grand romantic gesture. At the end, the lights dimmed, and Jay transitioned into his track "N****s in Paris" -- a pretty crazy transition, we gotta say.
